messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rafael had been a QA engineer for most of his adult life, a man used to checking details twice and trusting systems to behave predictably. That expectation had been shattered the summer the wildfire came through the edge of the neighborhood where he and his wife lived. He remembered the air first: hot, dry, and carrying a sharp smell of smoke that seemed to arrive before the flames were visible. From the kitchen window he had seen orange light licking up behind a line of houses, and when the wind shifted, the smell thickened until it felt like it was in his throat. The weather that day had been unnervingly similar to the conditions in which the fire had spread so quickly—still, hot, and deceptively calm—and that sameness has stayed with him. Even now, when smoke drifts from a neighbor’s grill or a brush fire is reported on the news, or when the afternoon turns dry and heavy in the same way, Rafael feels the old alarm rise before he can stop it.

In the months after the evacuation, those reminders set off a familiar chain of reactions. The smell of smoke, the sight of flames, or even a stretch of weather that felt too much like that day would send him into long bouts of self-blame and prevention-focused rumination. He would replay the event over and over, dwelling on what he had done wrong and what he should have noticed sooner, wondering whether he had left too late, packed too slowly, or missed some sign that the fire was moving closer. He could spend an evening silently working through alternate versions of the day, convinced that if he thought hard enough he might find the one decision that would have prevented everything. At times he tried to push the thoughts out of his mind altogether, forcing himself to turn the television up or bury himself in routine tasks at the house, but the harder he tried to shut them down, the more they seemed to gather force at the edges of his attention.

What made this pattern especially hard to break was how his body reacted whenever the memories were stirred. The moment a trigger hit, Rafael would feel his chest tighten, his heart pounding hard enough that he became acutely aware of it, and he would feel suddenly on edge, as if danger might be nearby again. He described himself as jumpy and easily startled; a door closing in the next room, the hiss of something heating on the stove, or a sudden movement in his peripheral vision could make him flinch before he had time to think. Those bodily surges made the disaster feel immediate rather than distant, and once he noticed them he became even more vigilant, scanning the air, the windows, the neighborhood, and the weather forecast for anything that might suggest smoke or fire. He found himself checking outside more often, watching the sky at dusk, and listening for news alerts, because if his body was warning him, he believed he had to stay watchful.

That watchfulness, however, began to make the reminders more frequent. Rafael noticed that once he was scanning for smoke or signs of fire, he started picking them up everywhere: the burnt smell from a passing car, a faint haze from a backyard fire pit, the orange glow of a sunset that resembled flames at the horizon. He had come to dread the summer heat and the thick, still afternoons because they seemed to invite the same vigilance all over again. The more he monitored for danger, the more cues he encountered, and each cue sent him back into the same pattern of trying to suppress the images while mentally revisiting what he had done and how the disaster might have been avoided. At home, this left him tense and irritable, and at work, even though he was no longer in the same active role as before, he noticed he was less able to concentrate when the building’s heating system gave off a faint burning odor or when someone mentioned a controlled burn. He would excuse himself, walk slowly around the office, and try to collect himself before returning, determined not to let the memories show.

Over time, the cycle narrowed his life. Rafael became more guarded in the house and around his neighborhood, and his wife noticed that he seemed to be waiting for something bad whenever the weather turned warm and still. He wanted to believe that keeping alert would keep him safe, but the effort left him exhausted and more sensitive to every smell, every flash of light, every change in the air. By the time he came to treatment, he was afraid that his mind would not stop replaying the fire and that his body would keep reacting as if the next smoke smell meant they were in danger again. He hoped for a way to feel ordinary weather, ordinary smells, and ordinary evenings without immediately being pulled back to that day.
